sentences.text: The attic at his grandfather's was reached by a ladder and had one bulb that had not worked since before Joaquim was born.
He went up in the dark on purpose.
That was the point of it.
In the dark his condition was irrelevant, because in the dark nobody has any edges, and for an hour a night he was exactly as capable as anybody else in the world, which is to say not very.
He sat with his back against a trunk and did nothing at all.
It was the only hour of his day in which nothing was being managed.
He would like that understood without it sounding like a complaint about his family, because it is not one.
Every single thing they did was the right thing and he would have done the same.

But there is a particular tiredness in being the object of continuous careful attention, and it does not go away by being grateful for the attention, and at thirteen he had no way at all of saying so.
In the dark of that attic he was not the boy whose eyes were going.
He was a person sitting in a dark room, which is a thing anybody can be, and it was restful in a way he has never quite got back.
He heard her on the fourth or fifth evening.
Not the flying — he had heard the flying from the first night and had assumed birds.
What he heard on the fourth or fifth evening, when he had been sitting still long enough, was the other thing.
It is a series of clicks and it is mostly too high for a person.
What comes down into human range is the low edge of it: a fast dry ticking, right at the top of what an ear will take, that goes across the room and comes back.
He could not hear all of it and he knows that now.

What reaches a thirteen-year-old ear is the bottom of the range and there was a great deal going on above it, and one of the strange satisfactions of his twenties has been putting equipment on that attic and finding out how much he had been missing.
At the time he had the low edge and it was enough.
She was working.
That is the word he arrived at and has never improved on.
It was not flapping about.
It was a search pattern — out along the ridge beam, down the gable, across, back — with the ticking speeding up whenever she came near anything and slowing when she was in open air.
Joaquim sat in the pitch dark of that attic and listened to something map a room.
It took perhaps forty seconds, which he timed on later evenings and which never varied by much.
Out, down, across, back.
Then a pause.
Then again, and the second pass was faster than the first, because by then she was not mapping — she was checking what had changed.
Nothing had changed.
Nothing changes in an attic.
She did it anyway, every night, for the whole of that spring and summer.
He did not move for a long time, and when he finally did, the ticking came at him fast and hard and then stopped and went away, and he understood that he had just been drawn.
